Author: @anthonyschroeder521
Content: Talking about the thermosiphon and saturation boiling curve.... there is one relatively important delta in most operational thermosiphons... That saturation curve is based on a static pressure. Obviously a sealed 2 phase system pressurizes as it heats up, which depresses boiling, as a result, in most small volume thermosiphons, the curve ends up smearing to the +x and +y direction. The larger your free volume in proportion to your evaporator (heat injection point), the less boiling depression you expect to see. With our small cu/water heatpipes, therefore, they are more tolerant to that excursion as boiling limit gets suppressed by pressure build up. This system has so much more condenser volume which limits the amount of pressurization you can get (and thus limits the boiling suppression you are looking for).

What they should do from a marketing standpoint, but also performance standpoint is to add some kind of screw/nob, that would tune the vibrations to the actual setup so that the vibrations are cancelled out the most with user adjustments.

Author: @tramapolean
Content: Very interesting info! But weird they are still grappling with Leidenfrost as this has been a known issue for CPU cooling for at least the three decades I have been doing liquid cooling. What is interesting is so many designs are still using a simple flow across the top of the surface, but there was a design where the cooled liquid was squirted into the hot plate, where there were matching holes for it, so the Leidenfrost effect could always be actively disrupted by the fresh coolant coming in. The issue for water is that any impurities in the loop inevitably block these micropipes, but given this is quite a different fluid (or maybe it isn't?) and a closed loop (although system porosity was mentioned), then does seem like there is room for more control over what is in the full loop. This could mean gunk buildup can be eliminated.

Content:
Jakob is awesome.

Phase change (boiling) engineering actually gets SUPER complicated because you have "micro" pockets of phase change happening, which causes all KINDS of problems.

(In boat propellers, localised boiling due to rapid changes of motion of the propeller itself, causes caviation (drop in pressure), which is enough to PHYSICALLY damage said propeller blades.)

You don't cover that in neither your 4th grade science classes nor even in your 3rd year thermo/fluid dynamics classes.

It is crazy/ridiculous how complicated the entire act of "boiling" can be.

(And then to model it accurately, people have literally gotten Ph.D.s just to study this thing called "boiling". You' never look at boiling potatoes nor making hard boiled eggs nor making ramen (in a pot), the same.)

Content: 20:21 The drop after CHF does not appear sharp in this heat flux vs. temperature log-log graph — or in the linear version of this plot. But in a heat flux vs. time graph, it can appear sharp: as heat flux decreases, less heat is removed, the surface temperature rises, and the situation worsens. It is "sharp" because of this feedback loop and not necessarily because of the graph’s scaling.

Author: @nexy84
Content:
Always good to see Noctua and Jakob Dellinger at Computex :)

However, it also seems that my predictions from last year, and comments that I made previously were also correct. Noctua, as a brand, can't survive by air coolers and case fans alone, especially when their products are so expensive for the sake of high thermal and noise performance. Their products might be chart toppers in performance, but when the competition is not far behind, yet their products can be purchased for a fraction of Noctua's price, many buyers will rightly ask themselves the question whether buying Noctua is good investment or not. There will be always people who are willing to pay a hefty price premium for the best, but plenty of others will buy something cheaper, like a Thermaltake air cooler instead.

Previously I predicted that Noctua will eventually need to extend its portfolio, and we can see this now by introducing a liquid AIO and really pushing for this thermosiphon solution, which they showed previously at Computex, yet they didn't know if it will be ever released. This is important, because trying as hard as they can, they can't beat liquid AIOs, which are often cheaper then Noctua's top air coolers.

Introducing a computer case with Antec (going with the Flux Pro was a very good choice IMHO) is also a a proof of expanding their portfolio.

This is a good approach IMHO, and I think Noctua is doing the right thing here.
Excelent editing as always! Thank you!
